note: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery, and the blue string of Rabbi Yonatan's ritual fringes was dragging over the graves. Rabbi Hiyya told him to lift it, so the dead would not say: Tomorrow they will be buried with us, and now they insult us. Rabbi Yonatan asked whether the dead know so much, quoting "the dead know nothing." Rabbi Hiyya answered that he had not read or understood the verse properly: "the living" who know they will die are the righteous, who are called living even in death. His explanation continues in the discussion that follows.
why: The Gemara is discussing the honor owed to the dead, such as not riding on their bones and escorting a funeral; this story asks whether the dead even know how they are treated.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who told his companion to lift his fringes so as not to insult the dead.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: A Sage whose fringes dragged over the graves, and who doubted the dead know anything.

terms.meaning: Tzitzit, the knotted strings worn on the corners of a garment as a commandment, which included a sky-blue thread.

note: A student asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer is optional (optional, he said) and then Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi (obligatory). Before the assembled Sages, Rabban Gamliel made Rabbi Yehoshua admit his view and left him standing through the lecture. The angry crowd halted the lecture and removed Rabban Gamliel, appointing eighteen-year-old Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, whose hair miraculously turned white. The doors opened to all students and hundreds of benches were added. Rabban Gamliel stayed in the study hall, then went to apologize; at Rabbi Yehoshua's soot-blackened house he learned he was a blacksmith. Forgiven for his father's sake, he was restored, lecturing three weeks to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's one.
why: The mishna says the evening prayer is not fixed, which the Gemara reads as optional, the very point Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua disputed; this teaching tells the confrontation that dispute led to.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the Sages, removed from office after humiliating Rabbi Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who held the evening prayer optional and was made to stand; a blacksmith by trade.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Appointed head of the yeshiva in Rabban Gamliel's place at eighteen.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage considered for the post, who later offered to restore Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The student whose question set off the whole incident.

terms.meaning: The president and leader of the Sages and of the community.
A name for the Torah scholars who do battle in debate in the study hall.
The person who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud so the whole audience could hear it.
Being allowed to marry a Jew by birth; the Torah forbids this to Ammonite converts.

note: Mar, son of Ravina, was once walking through a valley of willows and grew thirsty; a miracle happened and a spring of water appeared for him, and he drank. Another time, in the marketplace of Mehoza, a wild camel attacked him; a wall cracked open, he went inside it and was rescued. From then on, whenever he came to the willows or to the Mehoza marketplace, he recited a blessing thanking God who performed a miracle for him there, naming both miracles.
why: The Gemara has asked whether a blessing is said only for a miracle done for the whole people. Mar's practice shows an individual blesses for his own miracle, and the Sages conclude: everyone blesses for a public miracle, only the person himself for a private one.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Sage who was saved by two miracles, a spring in the willows and escape from a wild camel, and blessed God at both places.

terms.term: Blessed…Who performed a miracle for me
terms.meaning: A short blessing said when returning to a place where one was miraculously saved. The dots stand for the standard opening, Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe.

note: Rav Ketina was walking along a road and, as he reached the door of a necromancer, the ground rumbled in an earthquake. He wondered aloud whether the necromancer knew what the earthquake was. The necromancer called out, Ketina, Ketina, why would I not know? When God remembers His children suffering among the nations, He sheds two tears into the great sea, and the sound is heard from one end of the world to the other. Rav Ketina declared the necromancer a liar, since two tears should make two quakes; the Gemara remarks that there are in fact two, and Rav Ketina refused to admit it so that people would not be led astray after the necromancer.
why: The mishna requires a blessing over zeva'ot, and Rav Ketina defines the word as an earthquake. The story leads into a list of the Sages' explanations of what causes earthquakes, and then thunder and wind, all phenomena over which that blessing is said.

people.name: Rav Ketina
people.about: A Sage who defined zeva'ot as an earthquake and who met the necromancer on the road.

terms.meaning: Someone who claims to consult the dead. The Torah forbids this practice, which is why Rav Ketina would not let people credit what he said.
A word in the mishna for a natural event over which one says the blessing praising God whose strength and power fill the world. Rav Ketina explains it as earthquakes.

note: Rabbi Akiva came to a town and asked for lodging, but no one would give him any. He said, Everything God does is for the best, and slept in a field with his rooster, his donkey and a candle. The wind blew out the candle, a cat ate the rooster and a lion ate the donkey, and again he said, Everything God does is for the best. That night an army came and took the town captive; as the translation explains, he alone was saved, with no light, crowing rooster or donkey to give him away. He said, Didn't I tell you? Everything God does is for the best.
why: The Gemara has cited a teaching in Rabbi Akiva's name that a person should always train himself to say that everything God does is for the best. This story is told as the example of Rabbi Akiva living by his own teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who was refused lodging, lost his animals and light in the night, and was spared when the town was captured.
